claim: Staphylococcus aureus is a common colonizer of healthy skin and mucous membranes.
source: Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) is a common colonizer of healthy skin and mucous membranes.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by established scientific knowledge about S. aureus colonization patterns.

claim: S. aureus is the most frequent cause of skin and soft tissue infections.
source: At the same time, S. aureus is the most frequent cause of skin and soft tissue infections.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract based on established medical knowledge.

claim: Dermal macrophages are critical for the coordinated defense against invading S. aureus.
source: Dermal macrophages (Mφ) are critical for the coordinated defense against invading S. aureus, yet they have a limited life span with replacement by bone marrow derived monocytes.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work in the introduction section.

claim: Mice previously infected with S. aureus showed faster monocyte recruitment upon secondary infection.
source: In a strictly dermal infection model we found that mice, which were previously infected with S. aureus, showed faster monocyte recruitment, increased bacterial killing and improved healing upon a secondary infection.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically shown in Figure 1.

claim: Mice previously infected with S. aureus showed increased bacterial killing upon secondary infection.
source: In a strictly dermal infection model we found that mice, which were previously infected with S. aureus, showed faster monocyte recruitment, increased bacterial killing and improved healing upon a secondary infection.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by CFU data in Figure 1.

claim: Skin infection decreased macrophage half-life, thereby limiting the duration of memory.
source: However, skin infection decreased Mφ half-life, thereby limiting the duration of memory.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using PKH26 labeling and bone marrow chimera experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Resident dermal macrophages are programmed locally, independently of bone marrow-derived monocytes during staphylococcal skin infection.
source: In summary, resident dermal Mφ are programmed locally, independently of bone marrow-derived monocytes during staphylococcal skin infection leading to transiently increased resistance against a second infection.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by experiments in Ccr2-/- mice and bone marrow transfer experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: S. aureus causes severe invasive infections including osteomyelitis, endocarditis, pneumonia, and septicemia.
source: Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) is an important human pathogen, which causes severe invasive infections including osteomyelitis, endocarditis, pneumonia, and septicemia (Noskin et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Noskin et al., 2007.

claim: S. aureus stably colonizes the anterior nares and moist areas of the skin in up to 30% of healthy people.
source: On the other hand, S. aureus stably colonizes the anterior nares and moist areas of the skin in up to 30% of healthy people with a high fidelity of clones (Verhoeven et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Verhoeven et al., 2014.

claim: High frequencies of S. aureus-specific antibodies and circulating T cells do not safely protect from invasive infections.
source: However, in the case of S. aureus, high frequencies of S. aureus-specific antibodies and circulating T cells do not safely protect from invasive infections (Stentzel et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Stentzel et al., 2015.

claim: Humans and mice with global defects in lymphocyte development do not exhibit an exquisite susceptibility to S. aureus infection.
source: Moreover, humans and mice with global defects in lymphocyte development do not exhibit an exquisite susceptibility to S. aureus infection, despite the frequent encounters outlined above (Schmaler et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schmaler et al., 2011.

claim: Infections with S. aureus are a primary indicator of a deficiency in cellular innate immunity, specifically MyD88/IRAK4 deficiency and chronic granulomatous disease.
source: In contrast, infections with S. aureus are a primary indicator of a deficiency in cellular innate immunity, that is MyD88/IRAK4 deficiency and chronic granulomatous disease (Feuerstein et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Feuerstein et al., 2017.

claim: Macrophages are essential for the rapid and coordinated defense against S. aureus invading the skin.
source: Accordingly, several studies have identified Mφ as being essential for the rapid and coordinated defense against S. aureus invading the skin (Feuerstein et al., 2015; Abtin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Feuerstein et al., 2015 and Abtin et al., 2014.

claim: Priming with LPS boosts resistance to S. aureus 3 weeks after injection.
source: As an example, priming with LPS boosts resistance to S. aureus 3 weeks after injection (Yoshida et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yoshida et al., 2015.

claim: Staphylococcal soft tissue infections induce a more robust immune response to a second challenge.
source: More specifically, it was very recently reported that staphylococcal soft tissue infections induce a more robust immune response to a second challenge (Chan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chan et al., 2018.

claim: Mechanisms for the establishment of innate memory involve phosphorylation of the stress-response transcription factor ATF7.
source: Mechanisms for the establishment of innate memory involve phosphorylation of the stress-response transcription factor ATF7, epigenetic programming through histone modifications leading to stronger gene transcription upon re-stimulation as well as metabolic changes of Mφ via mTOR- and HIF-1α–mediated aerobic glycolysis (Yoshida et al., 2015; Cheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yoshida et al., 2015 and Cheng et al., 2014.

claim: Innate memory mechanisms involve epigenetic programming through histone modifications leading to stronger gene transcription upon re-stimulation.
source: Mechanisms for the establishment of innate memory involve phosphorylation of the stress-response transcription factor ATF7, epigenetic programming through histone modifications leading to stronger gene transcription upon re-stimulation as well as metabolic changes of Mφ via mTOR- and HIF-1α–mediated aerobic glycolysis (Yoshida et al., 2015; Cheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yoshida et al., 2015 and Cheng et al., 2014.

claim: Innate memory mechanisms involve metabolic changes of macrophages via mTOR- and HIF-1α–mediated aerobic glycolysis.
source: Mechanisms for the establishment of innate memory involve phosphorylation of the stress-response transcription factor ATF7, epigenetic programming through histone modifications leading to stronger gene transcription upon re-stimulation as well as metabolic changes of Mφ via mTOR- and HIF-1α–mediated aerobic glycolysis (Yoshida et al., 2015; Cheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yoshida et al., 2015 and Cheng et al., 2014.

claim: Primed mice had significantly increased bacterial killing compared to naïve mice 5 days after secondary infection.
source: Previous infection with S. aureus (primed) significantly increased bacterial killing and was associated with fewer neutrophils in the tissue 5 days after the 2nd infection (Figure 1B, Figure 1D).
evidence: This is directly supported by CFU data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Primed mice had fewer neutrophils in the tissue 5 days after secondary infection compared to naïve mice.
source: Previous infection with S. aureus (primed) significantly increased bacterial killing and was associated with fewer neutrophils in the tissue 5 days after the 2nd infection (Figure 1B, Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: CD64hi dermal macrophages were increased 3 weeks after primary S. aureus infection.
source: 3 weeks after primary S. aureus infection, that is immediately before the second infection, CD64hi dermal Mφ (gating strategy depicted in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) were increased (Figure 1C), whereas S. aureus could not be cultured and PML were virtually absent (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: S. aureus could not be cultured 3 weeks after primary infection.
source: 3 weeks after primary S. aureus infection, that is immediately before the second infection, CD64hi dermal Mφ (gating strategy depicted in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) were increased (Figure 1C), whereas S. aureus could not be cultured and PML were virtually absent (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Neutrophils were virtually absent 3 weeks after primary S. aureus infection.
source: 3 weeks after primary S. aureus infection, that is immediately before the second infection, CD64hi dermal Mφ (gating strategy depicted in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) were increased (Figure 1C), whereas S. aureus could not be cultured and PML were virtually absent (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Primed mice had less Ly6Chi skin macrophages compared to naïve mice 5 days after secondary infection.
source: In addition to the reduced number of neutrophils, primed mice had less Ly6Chi skin macrophages compared to naïve mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Ly6Chi CD64hi CX3CR1int skin macrophages are progeny of recruited Ly6Chi monocytes.
source: As shown in our previous work, Ly6Chi CD64hi CX3CR1int skin Mφ are progeny of recruited Ly6Chi monocytes and will eventually differentiate into resident Ly6Clo Mφ (Feuerstein et al., 2015; Kolter et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by Feuerstein et al., 2015 and Kolter et al., 2019.

claim: Ly6Chi CD64hi CX3CR1int skin macrophages will eventually differentiate into resident Ly6Clo macrophages.
source: As shown in our previous work, Ly6Chi CD64hi CX3CR1int skin Mφ are progeny of recruited Ly6Chi monocytes and will eventually differentiate into resident Ly6Clo Mφ (Feuerstein et al., 2015; Kolter et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by Feuerstein et al., 2015 and Kolter et al., 2019.

claim: Previously infected mice showed a slight increase of Ly6Clo dermal macrophages 24 hours after secondary infection.
source: In previously infected mice, we observed a slight increase of Ly6Clo dermal Mφ and an increase of Ly6Chi dermal Mφ already 24 hr after (re-)infection while by day 5 Ly6Chi dermal Mφ were lower in primed mice (Figure 1E, Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Previously infected mice showed an increase of Ly6Chi dermal macrophages 24 hours after secondary infection.
source: In previously infected mice, we observed a slight increase of Ly6Clo dermal Mφ and an increase of Ly6Chi dermal Mφ already 24 hr after (re-)infection while by day 5 Ly6Chi dermal Mφ were lower in primed mice (Figure 1E, Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Increased bacterial killing was already apparent one day after reinfection in primed mice.
source: However, increased bacterial killing was already apparent one day after reinfection (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Bacteria were no longer detectable 2 weeks after primary infection.
source: We found that bacteria were no longer detectable and that skin infiltrating PML, Ly6C expression and tissue edema were back to base line 2 weeks after infection (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Skin infiltrating neutrophils were back to baseline 2 weeks after primary infection.
source: We found that bacteria were no longer detectable and that skin infiltrating PML, Ly6C expression and tissue edema were back to base line 2 weeks after infection (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Ly6C expression was back to baseline 2 weeks after primary infection.
source: We found that bacteria were no longer detectable and that skin infiltrating PML, Ly6C expression and tissue edema were back to base line 2 weeks after infection (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Tissue edema was back to baseline 2 weeks after primary infection.
source: We found that bacteria were no longer detectable and that skin infiltrating PML, Ly6C expression and tissue edema were back to base line 2 weeks after infection (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Ccr2-/- mice exhibit an overall higher bacterial burden after primary S. aureus infection compared to wild-type mice.
source: First, we found naïve Ccr2-/- mice to exhibit an overall higher bacterial burden after primary S. aureus infection.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations in Ccr2-/- mice.

claim: Rechallenge of previously infected Ccr2-/- mice revealed increased bacterial killing compared to naïve counterparts.
source: However, a rechallenge of previously infected Ccr2-/- mice revealed increased bacterial killing (as indicated by a reduction in S. aureus CFU), decreased infiltrating PML, and less skin IL-1β concentrations as compared to naïve counterparts 5 days after (re-)infection (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by CFU, flow cytometry, and ELISA data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Rechallenge of previously infected Ccr2-/- mice revealed decreased infiltrating neutrophils compared to naïve counterparts.
source: However, a rechallenge of previously infected Ccr2-/- mice revealed increased bacterial killing (as indicated by a reduction in S. aureus CFU), decreased infiltrating PML, and less skin IL-1β concentrations as compared to naïve counterparts 5 days after (re-)infection (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Rechallenge of previously infected Ccr2-/- mice revealed less skin IL-1β concentrations compared to naïve counterparts.
source: However, a rechallenge of previously infected Ccr2-/- mice revealed increased bacterial killing (as indicated by a reduction in S. aureus CFU), decreased infiltrating PML, and less skin IL-1β concentrations as compared to naïve counterparts 5 days after (re-)infection (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Bone marrow transfer from primed to naïve mice did not transfer the memory phenotype.
source: In concordance with our previous finding that monocytes were not essential for innate memory after dermal S. aureus infection, we did not observe a significant difference in bacterial killing and neutrophil recruitment between recipient mice, which were reconstituted with bone marrow from infected mice, and those which were reconstituted with bone marrow from PBS treated mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by bone marrow chimera data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Primed Rag2–/–γc–/– mice showed increased bacterial killing compared to naïve Rag2–/–γc–/– mice.
source: Primed Rag2–/–γc–/– mice showed a clear memory phenotype with increased bacterial killing, reduced PML and IL-1β tissue concentration at 5 days p.i. (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Primed Rag2–/–γc–/– mice showed reduced neutrophils compared to naïve Rag2–/–γc–/– mice.
source: Primed Rag2–/–γc–/– mice showed a clear memory phenotype with increased bacterial killing, reduced PML and IL-1β tissue concentration at 5 days p.i. (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Primed Rag2–/–γc–/– mice showed reduced IL-1β tissue concentration compared to naïve Rag2–/–γc–/– mice.
source: Primed Rag2–/–γc–/– mice showed a clear memory phenotype with increased bacterial killing, reduced PML and IL-1β tissue concentration at 5 days p.i. (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The lasting protective effects exerted by S. aureus did not depend on bone-marrow derived monocytes and the adaptive immune system.
source: Therefore, the lasting protective effects exerted by S. aureus did not depend on bone-marrow derived monocytes and the adaptive immune system and qualified as 'innate immune memory'.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experiments in Ccr2-/- and Rag2–/–γc–/– mice shown in Figure 2.

claim: Liposomal clodronate depletes about 70–80% of all CD64hi dermal macrophages within 2 days.
source: This method depletes about 70–80% of all CD64hi dermal Mφ within 2 days by induction of apoptosis (Feuerstein et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Feuerstein et al., 2015.

claim: Repopulation of dermal macrophages occurred one week after clodronate depletion.
source: Repopulation of dermal Mφ occurred one week after depletion (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Depletion of resident dermal macrophages abolished innate memory.
source: We found reduced bacterial killing, increased PML numbers and higher IL-1β concentrations in the skin of clodronate treated mice (Figure 3C). This indicated that depletion of the resident dermal Mφ pool abolished innate memory, although the Mφ density was maintained due to invasion of monocytes.
evidence: This is supported by CFU, flow cytometry, and ELISA data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Innate memory could only be observed after a re-challenge of the same ear, not the contralateral ear.
source: Interestingly, innate memory could only be observed after a re-challenge of the same ear (Figure 3D), indicating that it was primarily mediated by local resident Mφ without contribution of blood- or bone marrow-derived cells.
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Innate memory was primarily mediated by local resident macrophages without contribution of blood- or bone marrow-derived cells.
source: Interestingly, innate memory could only be observed after a re-challenge of the same ear (Figure 3D), indicating that it was primarily mediated by local resident Mφ without contribution of blood- or bone marrow-derived cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that memory was local to the infected ear.

claim: Three weeks after S. aureus infection, 65 genes were differentially expressed in dermal macrophages compared to vehicle control.
source: Three weeks after S. aureus infection, 65 genes were differentially expressed as compared to Mφ from vehicle control mice including the transcription factor Stat1 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Gene ontology analysis revealed enrichment of terms associated with antigen presentation, response to interferons and positive regulation of cytokine production in primed dermal macrophages.
source: Gene ontology analysis using the Panther bioinformatics platform revealed enrichment of terms associated with antigen presentation, response to interferons and positive regulation of cytokine production (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Intradermal S. aureus infection induced lasting changes in a distinct subset of genes associated with increased resistance to secondary infection.
source: Accordingly, intradermal S. aureus infection induced lasting changes in a distinct subset of genes which was associated with increased resistance to secondary infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the microarray data and functional experiments.

claim: Upregulation of Stat1 was confirmed by quantitative PCR in sorted CD64hi macrophages from primed mice.
source: Upregulation of the transcription factor Stat1, as observed in the gene expression array, and its target Cxcl9, was confirmed by quantitative PCR to be increased in sorted CD64hi Mφ from wt mice previously infected with S. aureus as compared to naïve mice (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Upregulation of Cxcl9 was confirmed by quantitative PCR in sorted CD64hi macrophages from primed mice.
source: Upregulation of the transcription factor Stat1, as observed in the gene expression array, and its target Cxcl9, was confirmed by quantitative PCR to be increased in sorted CD64hi Mφ from wt mice previously infected with S. aureus as compared to naïve mice (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Stat1 and Cxcl9 have been shown to be involved in innate memory in LPS-primed macrophages.
source: These genes have been shown to be involved in innate memory in LPS-primed Mφ, which also show an enhanced resistance to S. aureus after 3 weeks (Yoshida et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yoshida et al., 2015.

claim: Phosphorylated STAT1 was increased in dermal macrophages from whole tissue lysates of S. aureus infected skin.
source: Accordingly, phosphorylated STAT1 was increased in dermal Mφ from whole tissue lysates of S. aureus infected skin (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Macrophages of previously infected mice had increased expression of Stat1 and Cxcl9 1 and 5 days after reinfection.
source: Furthermore, Mφ of previously infected mice had increased expression of Stat1 and Cxcl9 1 and 5 days after (re-)infection (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Increased concentrations of CXCL9 were detectable 5 days after reinfection in skin lysates of primed mice compared to naïve controls.
source: In addition, increased concentrations of CXCL9 were detectable 5 days after (re-)infection in skin lysates of primed mice compared to naïve controls (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: CXCL9 has been reported to exhibit direct antimicrobial activity independent of its chemotactic activity.
source: Notably, CXCL9 has been reported to exhibit direct antimicrobial activity independent of its chemotactic activity (Reid-Yu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Reid-Yu et al., 2015.

claim: CXCL9 exhibits direct killing capacity on S. aureus strain Newman in vitro.
source: We confirmed this observation by an in vitro S. aureus killing assay showing the direct killing capacity of CXCL9 on the S. aureus strain Newman (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro killing assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In dermal macrophages sorted from primed mice that had received clodronate, the enhanced expression of Stat1 and Cxcl9 was lost.
source: Notably, in dermal Mφ sorted from primed mice that had received clodronate (as in Figure 3A), the enhanced expression of Stat1 and Cxcl9 was lost (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Dermal macrophages from primed mice showed higher pro-IL1B expression than macrophages from naïve mice when stimulated ex vivo with fixed S. aureus.
source: We found that dermal Mφ from primed mice showed higher pro IL1B expression and more TNF-α production than Mφ from naïve mice (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Dermal macrophages from primed mice showed more TNF-α production than macrophages from naïve mice when stimulated ex vivo with fixed S. aureus.
source: We found that dermal Mφ from primed mice showed higher pro IL1B expression and more TNF-α production than Mφ from naïve mice (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: In vivo priming leads to increased responsiveness to the same pathogen at the single macrophage level.
source: This finding suggested that in vivo priming leads to increased responsiveness to the same pathogen at the single Mφ level.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ex vivo stimulation experiments.

claim: Upon challenge of primed mice for 4 hours with fixed S. aureus, significantly more skin-infiltrating neutrophils and Ly6Chi macrophages were observed.
source: Upon challenge of primed mice for 4 hr with fixed S. aureus (Figure 5G), we observed significantly more skin-infiltrating PML and Ly6Chi Mφ (Figure 5H) and visible skin erythema in previously infected mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Primed mice had increased concentrations of CXCL1 in whole tissue lysates compared to naïve counterparts after challenge with fixed S. aureus.
source: In full agreement with the above results, primed mice had increased concentrations of CXCL1 in whole tissue lysates compared to naïve counterparts (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The initial response to S. aureus primed macrophages for an increased responsiveness to the second infection resulting in more rapid recruitment of peripheral blood cells.
source: This strongly suggested that the initial response to S. aureus primed Mφ for an increased responsiveness to the second infection resulting in the more rapid recruitment of peripheral blood cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of increased cell recruitment in primed mice.

claim: Both CX3CR1lo Ly6Clo resident macrophages and CX3CR1int Ly6Chi macrophages exhibited increased expression of Stat1 and Cxcl9 compared to cells sorted from naïve mice.
source: We found both subsets to exhibit increased expression of Stat1 and Cxcl9 compared to cells sorted from naïve mice.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The expression of Stat1 and Cxcl9 was higher in the Ly6Chi subset compared to the Ly6Clo subset.
source: Interestingly, the expression of both genes was higher in the Ly6Chi subset, indicating that, while innate memory occurs in the absence of incoming Ly6Chi Mφ, these cells can also be primed in the microenvironment of the infected ear (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Incoming Ly6Chi macrophages can be primed in the microenvironment of the infected ear.
source: Interestingly, the expression of both genes was higher in the Ly6Chi subset, indicating that, while innate memory occurs in the absence of incoming Ly6Chi Mφ, these cells can also be primed in the microenvironment of the infected ear (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Ly6Chi cells show increased expression of memory markers.

claim: S. aureus did not prime bone marrow-derived macrophages for an enhanced secondary response in vitro.
source: Surprisingly, we did not find S. aureus to prime Mφ from different sources (bone-marrow, peritoneal cavity) for an enhanced secondary response in vitro as established for other effectors (Schrum et al., 2018; Cheng et al., 2014; Ifrim et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on in vitro experiments with bone marrow-derived macrophages.

claim: S. aureus did not prime peritoneal macrophages for an enhanced secondary response in vitro.
source: Surprisingly, we did not find S. aureus to prime Mφ from different sources (bone-marrow, peritoneal cavity) for an enhanced secondary response in vitro as established for other effectors (Schrum et al., 2018; Cheng et al., 2014; Ifrim et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on in vitro experiments with peritoneal macrophages.

claim: The induction of innate memory in vivo requires distinct cues from the infected tissue.
source: This indicated that the induction of innate memory in vivo requires distinct cues from the infected tissue, although monocytes and adaptive immune cells are not involved (see above).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that in vitro priming failed while in vivo priming succeeded.

claim: Primed Myd88-/- mice had reduced bacterial burden compared to naïve Myd88-/- mice.
source: Strikingly, primed Myd88-/- mice had reduced bacterial burden and increased expression of Stat1 and Cxcl9 compared to naïve mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Primed Myd88-/- mice had increased expression of Stat1 and Cxcl9 compared to naïve Myd88-/- mice.
source: Strikingly, primed Myd88-/- mice had reduced bacterial burden and increased expression of Stat1 and Cxcl9 compared to naïve mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Dermal macrophages from primed Myd88-/- mice exhibited a robust pro-IL1β response after S. aureus ex vivo stimulation.
source: Furthermore, dermal Mφ from primed mice exhibited a robust pro-IL1β response after S. aureus ex vivo stimulation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Innate S. aureus memory seems to be, at least partially, independent of MyD88.
source: The above results indicate that innate S. aureus memory seems to be, at least partially, independent of MyD88.
evidence: This is an inference based on experiments in Myd88-/- mice.

claim: Skin colonization with S. aureus led to a 50% increase in the frequency of Ly6Chi macrophages after infection of sDMDMm2 mice.
source: Skin colonization with S. aureus led to a 50% increase in the frequency of Ly6Chi Mφ after infection of sDMDMm2 mice while it did not affect the abundance of infection-induced PML (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Skin colonization with S. aureus did not affect the abundance of infection-induced neutrophils in sDMDMm2 mice.
source: Skin colonization with S. aureus led to a 50% increase in the frequency of Ly6Chi Mφ after infection of sDMDMm2 mice while it did not affect the abundance of infection-induced PML (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: S. aureus colonization slightly increases the response to subsequent infection, but does not induce an immunological memory similar to a dermal infection.
source: Thus, S. aureus colonization slightly increases the response to subsequent infection, but does not induce an immunological memory similar to a dermal infection with the same organism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of colonization and infection effects.

claim: The innate memory signature (increased expression of Stat1 and Cxcl9) was lost after 6 weeks.
source: Already after 6 weeks, the innate memory signature, that is the increased expression of Stat1 and its target gene Cxcl9 were lost (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Increased bacterial killing was lost in wild-type mice 6 weeks after primary infection.
source: Furthermore, increased bacterial killing was lost in wt mice 6 weeks after infection (Figure 6E, left panel).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: S. aureus infection decreased the half-life of dermal macrophages from an estimated 35 days to 10 days.
source: Compared to uninfected mice, S. aureus infection decreased the half-life of dermal Mφ from an estimated 35 days to 10 days, that is by around 70%.
evidence: This is based on PKH26 labeling experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: An increased replacement of the resident dermal macrophage pool by donor derived cells was observed up to six weeks after S. aureus infection in bone marrow chimeras.
source: Compared to uninfected mice, an increased replacement of the resident dermal Mφ pool by donor derived cells was observed up to six weeks after S. aureus infection (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by bone marrow chimera data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Increased bacterial killing could be observed in Ccr2-/- mice following secondary infection in mice that had been primed 6 weeks previously.
source: Indeed, increased bacterial killing could be observed in Ccr2-/- mice following secondary infection in mice that had been primed 6 weeks previously (Figure 6E, right panel), while no difference in PML numbers was observed between primed and naïve mice (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: S. aureus-induced innate memory is a transient phenomenon, which is lost within 6 to 12 weeks due to the replacement of resident macrophages by monocyte-derived macrophages.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that S. aureus-induced innate memory is a transient phenomenon, which is lost within 6 to 12 weeks due the replacement of resident Mφ by monocyte-derived Mφ (model depicted in Figure 7).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experiments showing loss of memory markers and function over time.

claim: Staphylococcal skin infection directly induced a memory signature in individual dermal macrophages, signified by the increased expression of STAT1 and CXCL9.
source: We found that staphylococcal skin infection directly induced a memory signature in individual dermal Mφ, signified by the increased expression of STAT1 and CXCL9, but at the same time increased Mφ turnover by naive bone-marrow derived cells, which eventually extinguished the memory.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Staphylococcal skin infection increased macrophage turnover by naive bone-marrow derived cells, which eventually extinguished the memory.
source: We found that staphylococcal skin infection directly induced a memory signature in individual dermal Mφ, signified by the increased expression of STAT1 and CXCL9, but at the same time increased Mφ turnover by naive bone-marrow derived cells, which eventually extinguished the memory.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Tissue resident dermal macrophages are programmed independently of bone marrow-derived monocytes during staphylococcal skin infection to mediate increased resistance against a second infection.
source: In summary, tissue resident dermal Mφ are programmed independently of bone marrow-derived monocytes during staphylococcal skin infection to mediate increased resistance against a second infection.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The infection-induced turnover of resident skin macrophages limits the duration of the innate memory response.
source: However, the infection-induced turnover of resident skin Mφ limits the duration of this innate memory response.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Macrophages downmodulate the response to endotoxin after exposure, a phenomenon called tolerance.
source: Accordingly, it has been appreciated for over 50 years that Mφ downmodulate the response to endotoxin after exposure, a phenomenon called tolerance (Greisman and Hornick, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Greisman and Hornick, 1975.

claim: Microbial components like β-glucan and LPS, and microorganisms such as yeast, vaccine strain mycobacteria and herpes viruses have been found to reprogram macrophages.
source: Notably, much of the groundwork was done in vitro, and microbial components like β-glucan and LPS, and microorganisms, such as yeast, vaccine strain mycobacteria and herpes viruses have been found to reprogram Mφ (Quintin et al., 2012; Yoshida et al., 2015; Kleinnijenhuis et al., 2012; Saeed et al., 2014; Barton et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: S. aureus has been shown to induce a macrophage dependent protective immunity in a penetrating skin and skin structure infection.
source: Very recently S. aureus has also been shown to induce a Mφ dependent protective immunity in a penetrating skin and skin structure infection (Chan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chan et al., 2018.

claim: The intradermal infection model recapitulates the initiation of the immune response by resident dermal macrophages, the recruitment of neutrophils and monocytes to the site of infection, the killing of bacteria and the contraction of inflammation without measurable circulation of bacteria and cytokines.
source: This model recapitulates the initiation of the immune response by resident dermal Mφ, the recruitment of PML and monocytes to the site of infection, the killing of bacteria and the contraction of inflammation without measurable circulation of bacteria and cytokines, and without effect on the mouse wellbeing (Feuerstein et al., 2017; Feuerstein et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Feuerstein et al., 2017 and Feuerstein et al., 2015.

claim: The intradermal infection model differs sharply from subcutaneous S. aureus infections, which lead to strong inflammation, large abscesses, dermonecrosis and bacterial dissemination to organs.
source: Thus, it differs sharply from subcutaneous S. aureus infections, which lead to strong inflammation, large abscesses, dermonecrosis and bacterial dissemination to organs like the spleen, kidney and liver (Chan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chan et al., 2018.

claim: S. aureus bacteria have been found to survive in osteoblasts from mice for months.
source: In the case of S. aureus, bacteria have been found to survive in osteoblasts from mice for months (Tuchscherr et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tuchscherr et al., 2015.

claim: Intradermal S. aureus infection led to persistent transcriptional changes in only 65 genes compared to vehicle control.
source: The transcriptional effects of dermal Mφ memory in situ were rather subtle, since intradermal S. aureus infection led to persistent transcriptional changes in only 65 genes compared to vehicle control.
evidence: This is based on microarray data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The immediate innate immune response is fully resolved 2 weeks after infection in the intradermal model.
source: It appears that the immediate innate immune response is fully resolved 2 weeks after infection in our model, as indicated by the absence of culturable bacteria, of skin infiltrating PML and of type I cytokines in the tissue at this stage.
evidence: This is based on CFU, flow cytometry, and cytokine data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: STAT1 appears to play a dominant role among the signaling intermediates implicated in macrophage memory.
source: Among the signaling intermediates, metabolic and epigenetic changes which have been previously implicated in Mφ memory (Quintin et al., 2012; Yoshida et al., 2015; Cheng et al., 2014; Saeed et al., 2014) STAT1 appears to play a dominant role (Yoshida et al., 2015; Saeed et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yoshida et al., 2015 and Saeed et al., 2014.

claim: CXCL9 possesses direct antimicrobial activity independent of its chemotactic activity.
source: It is intriguing that the STAT1-dependent chemokine CXCL9 possess direct antimicrobial activity independent of its chemotactic activity (Reid-Yu et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Reid-Yu et al., 2015 and Yang et al., 2003.

claim: A decline in β-glucan induced memory in vivo was observed in a similar time span (around 6 weeks) by Garcia-Valtanen et al.
source: This finding is in line with data from Garcia-Valtanen et al., who observed a decline in the β-glucan induced memory in vivo in a similar time span (Garcia-Valtanen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Garcia-Valtanen et al., 2017.

claim: Innate memory appears to require terminally differentiated macrophages in the tissue environment.
source: In other words, innate memory appears to require terminally differentiated Mφ in the tissue environment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that in vitro priming of bone marrow and peritoneal macrophages failed.

claim: Nucleic acids from S. aureus can be found in the non-lesional dermis of up to 30% of people.
source: However, the physical barrier of the epidermis appears to be less tight than commonly thought, since nucleic acids from S. aureus can be found in the non-lesional dermis of up to 30% of people (Crisp et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Crisp et al., 2015.

claim: Alveolar macrophages are primed in local adenovirus infections.
source: This local recall phenomenon is reminiscent of the recently reported priming of alveolar Mφ in local adenovirus infections (Yao et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yao et al., 2018.

claim: Microorganisms with an intracellular lifestyle and limited virulence, for example mycobacteria, may induce innate memory of cells in central components like hematopoietic stem cells.
source: In contrast, microorganisms with an intracellular lifestyle and limited virulence, for example mycobacteria, may induce innate memory of cells in central components like hematopoietic stem cells in order to allow for individual adaptations in host resistance (Kaufmann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kaufmann et al., 2018.
